A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

tools.name: DeferredToolPlaceholder
tools.description: Reserved placeholder that keeps deferred tool loading active; never call this tool.

tools.name: mcp__conductor__AskUserQuestion

question.description: The question to ask the user

options.description: Up to 4 options for the user to choose from. Do not include 'Other' - it is automatically provided.

header.description: Short label displayed above the question.

multiSelect.description: If true, user can select multiple options. Answers are comma-separated.

# Releasing Brain

Brain releases the same way Graph does: a tag triggers a build of every target,
the binaries and their checksums are attached to a GitHub release, and a nightly
prerelease is cut from `main` each morning.

## Cutting a release

1. Move the work into a `## [X.Y.Z]` section in `CHANGELOG.md`, dated.
2. Tag and push:

   ```sh
   git tag vX.Y.Z
   git push origin vX.Y.Z
   ```

`.github/workflows/release.yml` does the rest: it builds `linux`, `darwin`, and
`windows` for both `amd64` and `arm64`, packages each as a `.tar.gz` (`.zip` on
Windows), writes `checksums.txt`, and creates the release with generated notes.
Re-running it against an existing tag updates that release rather than failing.

You can also run it from the Actions tab with a version, which is the way to
re-cut a release whose upload failed.

### Why one runner builds everything

Brain's default build is pure Go — both the SQLite driver and the vector path
have cgo-free implementations (`internal/cli/sqlite_driver_purego.go`,
`internal/cli/embed_vec_purego.go`), and SQLite itself comes from
`modernc.org/sqlite` rather than a C binding — so `CGO_ENABLED=0`
cross-compiles every target from one Linux runner.
Graph needs a runner per OS because its tree-sitter bindings need cgo. The
release workflow asserts this rather than assuming it:

```yaml
- name: Verify the default build needs no cgo
  run: CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /dev/null ./cmd/entire-brain
```

If someone adds a cgo dependency to the default build, that step fails and the
release stops, instead of silently producing binaries that only run on the
build host.

The `brain_cgo` build tag still exists for the native embedder. It is not part
of a release build.

### Windows verification

Cross-compiling from one runner means the release path never executes a
Windows binary, and `test.yml`'s Windows suite runs with `CGO_ENABLED=1`
because the race detector needs cgo — not the pure-Go configuration that
ships. Both `release.yml` and `nightly.yml` therefore gate publishing on a
`verify windows` job on a Depot Windows runner (hosted `windows-latest` is
2-core on private repos and cannot finish `internal/cli` in one binary within
a reasonable budget — note this puts a Depot dependency on the publish path):
it runs `go test ./...` with
`CGO_ENABLED=0` and smoke-runs the CLI (`version`, `capabilities --json`, a
`remember`/`recall` roundtrip in a scratch repo) via `tools/windows-sanity.ps1`.
The release job runs the script against the actual `windows/amd64` artifact it
is about to publish; the nightly verifies its own equivalent build, because the
nightly builds and publishes in a single job. `windows/arm64` is still only
cross-compiled — no amd64 runner can execute it.

## Nightlies

`.github/workflows/nightly.yml` runs at 06:00 UTC, matching Graph, and tags
`vX.Y.Z-nightly.<timestamp>.<sha>` where `X.Y.Z` is the newest version in the
changelog.

It skips days `main` has not moved. A dated prerelease that is byte-identical to
yesterday's makes "which nightly has the fix" harder to answer, not easier, so
the run checks whether the newest prerelease already points at `HEAD` and exits
if it does.

## Pull requests build the release path

`release.yml` also runs on pull requests that change it. That run builds every
target and skips the publish job, so a change to the release process is proven
on the PR rather than on the tag that depends on it.

## What may be claimed in release material

`mise run release:readiness` reports which claims the retained evidence
supports. It classifies every track as one of `proven`, `local-gated`,
`pending-retained-proof`, `pending-target-evidence`, or `no-claim`, and the gate
fails when release material asserts something the evidence does not carry.

Run it before writing an announcement, and treat anything short of `proven` as
not sayable.

## Install channels

Releases reach users three ways:

| channel | resolves through |
|---|---|
| `entire plugin install brain` | the [plugin index](https://github.com/entireio/plugin-index) |
| `scripts/get-brain.sh` | the GitHub releases API, verifying `checksums.txt` |
| a downloaded archive | the release page |

The installer verifies the downloaded archive against `checksums.txt` and exits
non-zero on a mismatch. A missing checksum file is a warning; a wrong checksum
is fatal.

1	# Releasing Brain
2	
3	Brain releases the same way Graph does: a tag triggers a build of every target,
4	the binaries and their checksums are attached to a GitHub release, and a nightly
5	prerelease is cut from `main` each morning.
6	
7	## Cutting a release
8	
9	1. Move the work into a `## [X.Y.Z]` section in `CHANGELOG.md`, dated.
10	2. Tag and push:
11	
12	   ```sh
13	   git tag vX.Y.Z
14	   git push origin vX.Y.Z
15	   ```
16	
17	`.github/workflows/release.yml` does the rest: it builds `linux`, `darwin`, and
18	`windows` for both `amd64` and `arm64`, packages each as a `.tar.gz` (`.zip` on
19	Windows), writes `checksums.txt`, and creates the release with generated notes.
20	Re-running it against an existing tag updates that release rather than failing.
21	
22	You can also run it from the Actions tab with a version, which is the way to
23	re-cut a release whose upload failed.
24	
25	### Why one runner builds everything
26	
27	Brain's default build is pure Go — both the SQLite driver and the vector path
28	have cgo-free implementations (`internal/cli/sqlite_driver_purego.go`,
29	`internal/cli/embed_vec_purego.go`), and SQLite itself comes from
30	`modernc.org/sqlite` rather than a C binding — so `CGO_ENABLED=0`
31	cross-compiles every target from one Linux runner.
32	Graph needs a runner per OS because its tree-sitter bindings need cgo. The
33	release workflow asserts this rather than assuming it:
34	
35	```yaml
36	- name: Verify the default build needs no cgo
37	  run: CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /dev/null ./cmd/entire-brain
38	```
39	
40	If someone adds a cgo dependency to the default build, that step fails and the
41	release stops, instead of silently producing binaries that only run on the
42	build host.
43	
44	The `brain_cgo` build tag still exists for the native embedder. It is not part
45	of a release build.
46	
47	### Windows verification
48	
49	Cross-compiling from one runner means the release path never executes a
50	Windows binary, and `test.yml`'s Windows suite runs with `CGO_ENABLED=1`
51	because the race detector needs cgo — not the pure-Go configuration that
52	ships. Both `release.yml` and `nightly.yml` therefore gate publishing on a
53	`verify windows` job on a Depot Windows runner (hosted `windows-latest` is
54	2-core on private repos and cannot finish `internal/cli` in one binary within
55	a reasonable budget — note this puts a Depot dependency on the publish path):
56	it runs `go test ./...` with
57	`CGO_ENABLED=0` and smoke-runs the CLI (`version`, `capabilities --json`, a
58	`remember`/`recall` roundtrip in a scratch repo) via `tools/windows-sanity.ps1`.
59	The release job runs the script against the actual `windows/amd64` artifact it
60	is about to publish; the nightly verifies its own equivalent build, because the
61	nightly builds and publishes in a single job. `windows/arm64` is still only
62	cross-compiled — no amd64 runner can execute it.
63	
64	## Nightlies
65	
66	`.github/workflows/nightly.yml` runs at 06:00 UTC, matching Graph, and tags
67	`vX.Y.Z-nightly.<timestamp>.<sha>` where `X.Y.Z` is the newest version in the
68	changelog.
69	
70	It skips days `main` has not moved. A dated prerelease that is byte-identical to
71	yesterday's makes "which nightly has the fix" harder to answer, not easier, so
72	the run checks whether the newest prerelease already points at `HEAD` and exits
73	if it does.
74	
75	## Pull requests build the release path
76	
77	`release.yml` also runs on pull requests that change it. That run builds every
78	target and skips the publish job, so a change to the release process is proven
79	on the PR rather than on the tag that depends on it.
80	
81	## What may be claimed in release material
82	
83	`mise run release:readiness` reports which claims the retained evidence
84	supports. It classifies every track as one of `proven`, `local-gated`,
85	`pending-retained-proof`, `pending-target-evidence`, or `no-claim`, and the gate
86	fails when release material asserts something the evidence does not carry.
87	
88	Run it before writing an announcement, and treat anything short of `proven` as
89	not sayable.
90	
91	## Install channels
92	
93	Releases reach users three ways:
94	
95	| channel | resolves through |
96	|---|---|
97	| `entire plugin install brain` | the [plugin index](https://github.com/entireio/plugin-index) |
98	| `scripts/get-brain.sh` | the GitHub releases API, verifying `checksums.txt` |
99	| a downloaded archive | the release page |
100	
101	The installer verifies the downloaded archive against `checksums.txt` and exits
102	non-zero on a mismatch. A missing checksum file is a warning; a wrong checksum
103	is fatal.
104

# Changelog

All notable changes to `entire-brain` are recorded here. The format follows
[Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/).

## [Unreleased]

## [0.3.0] - 2026-10-26

### Removed

- The one-time migrations for Brain's old code stores. Refresh, code inspection,
  and bundle operations now refuse old layouts with recovery instructions;
  status and doctor report the same problem. Run `entire brain refresh index`
  with entire-brain 0.2.0 once before upgrading to preserve runtime traces, or
  back up and remove the brain directory and refresh to rebuild. Legacy vector
  detection remains in place for health and privacy checks.

### Changed

- Releases no longer re-prove retained performance evidence at tag time. The
  `release-evidence` job moved from the `test` workflow (where it ran on `v*`
  tags and blocked publishing) to a dispatch-only `evidence` workflow. Evidence
  is a point-in-time record: each manifest names the `source_head` it measured,
  every `mise run <lane>:evidence:update` audits with `--fail-on-flags` before
  writing reports, and the timed distill lanes' corpora are machine-bound, so
  re-measuring at every tag made releases wait on measurements the release did
  not change. Tagging now only builds, verifies, and publishes binaries.

- Re-recorded the Radar tool-contract evidence and the current-repo distill
  scheduler evidence against current main (median 1.89x of five pairs vs the
  1.25x floor, measured on a fresh zero-fact store so reconcile stays quiet).
  The large-repo distill lane still carries its September record; its corpus
  (a 2,375-session local brain store) exists only on the original recorder's
  machine.

### Fixed

- The sessions export no longer stalls for hours on a host CLI whose remote
  metadata fetch times out per checkpoint (entireio/cli#2902: 319 routed
  checkpoints × a 120s fetch deadline read as a `setup` hang). After three
  consecutive `checkpoint explain` reads each over 60 seconds, a circuit
  breaker stops asking, folds every skipped checkpoint into one counted
  warning naming the cause and the remedy, and the export finishes degraded
  in minutes. Validation tracked in COR-2277.

- A first `setup` no longer ends on `freshness: degraded`. The agent wiring
  files setup itself writes — `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, and the PreToolUse
  entry in `.claude/settings.json` — no longer count as a dirty worktree in the
  live state report, the same exemption the dirty-worktree gate already
  applied. The files stay in the indexed corpus.

- `status --fail-on degraded` and `--fail-on unsafe` no longer pass without
  looking when the brain has no semantic assessment: a degraded or unsafe
  retrieval freshness now trips the gate even when no graph provider is
  installed. A healthy retrieval report still does not substitute for the
  missing assessment, so `--fail-on release` keeps failing on unindexed brains.

- `mise run release:smoke` leg 1 gates on `--fail-on release` instead of
  `--fail-on degraded`, so a runner without the entire-graph provider fails
---TASKS---
smoke
lint
release

# Changelog

All notable changes to `entire-brain` are recorded here. The format follows
[Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/).

## [Unreleased]

## [0.3.0] - 2026-10-26

### Removed

- The one-time migrations for Brain's old code stores. Refresh, code inspection,
  and bundle operations now refuse old layouts with recovery instructions;
  status and doctor report the same problem. Run `entire brain refresh index`
  with entire-brain 0.2.0 once before upgrading to preserve runtime traces, or
  back up and remove the brain directory and refresh to rebuild. Legacy vector
  detection remains in place for health and privacy checks.

### Changed

- Releases no longer re-prove retained performance evidence at tag time. The
  `release-evidence` job moved from the `test` workflow (where it ran on `v*`
  tags and blocked publishing) to a dispatch-only `evidence` workflow. Evidence
  is a point-in-time record: each manifest names the `source_head` it measured,
  every `mise run <lane>:evidence:update` audits with `--fail-on-flags` before
  writing reports, and the timed distill lanes' corpora are machine-bound, so
  re-measuring at every tag made releases wait on measurements the release did
  not change. Tagging now only builds, verifies, and publishes binaries.

- Re-recorded the Radar tool-contract evidence and the current-repo distill
  scheduler evidence against current main (median 1.89x of five pairs vs the
  1.25x floor, measured on a fresh zero-fact store so reconcile stays quiet).
  The large-repo distill lane still carries its September record; its corpus
  (a 2,375-session local brain store) exists only on the original recorder's
  machine.

### Fixed

- The sessions export no longer stalls for hours on a host CLI whose remote
  metadata fetch times out per checkpoint (entireio/cli#2902: 319 routed
  checkpoints × a 120s fetch deadline read as a `setup` hang). After three
  consecutive `checkpoint explain` reads each over 60 seconds, a circuit
  breaker stops asking, folds every skipped checkpoint into one counted
  warning naming the cause and the remedy, and the export finishes degraded
  in minutes. Validation tracked in COR-2277.

- A first `setup` no longer ends on `freshness: degraded`. The agent wiring
  files setup itself writes — `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, and the PreToolUse
  entry in `.claude/settings.json` — no longer count as a dirty worktree in the
  live state report, the same exemption the dirty-worktree gate already
  applied. The files stay in the indexed corpus.

- `status --fail-on degraded` and `--fail-on unsafe` no longer pass without
  looking when the brain has no semantic assessment: a degraded or unsafe
  retrieval freshness now trips the gate even when no graph provider is
  installed. A healthy retrieval report still does not substitute for the
  missing assessment, so `--fail-on release` keeps failing on unindexed brains.

- `mise run release:smoke` leg 1 gates on `--fail-on release` instead of
  `--fail-on degraded`, so a runner without the entire-graph provider fails

#!/bin/bash
#MISE description="Release smoke: full user journey on scratch repos (enable, capture, distill, recall, graph, hosted sync up/down)"
#
# A tripwire, not a test suite: one assert per leg, each fails loudly.
# Legs: 1 setup, 2 checkpoint capture, 3 distill, 4 recall, 5 graph query,
#        6 hosted upload (staging), 7 pull+merge on a second clone.
#
# The entire-brain binary under test is built from this checkout (the RC SHA);
# the host `entire` CLI and the entire-graph provider are the installed ones.
# Brain state is isolated per "machine" via ENTIRE_PLUGIN_*_DIR, like
# scripts/hosted-sync-smoke.sh; HOME and the host CLI's login stay real because
# legs 3 and 6 need the real coding agent and the real staging auth.
#
# Environment the runner must export (legs 6-7; never hardcode secrets):
#   REPO_ID       region-local repo ULID of a STAGING brainstore repo
#   API_URL       that repo's home-cell base URL, e.g. https://<home-cell>.api.partial.to/api/v1
#   AUTH_CONTEXT  optional saved `entire auth` login to mint the token from
#                 (e.g. us.auth.partial.to); default: the active context
#   ENTIRE_BRAIN_BIN  optional prebuilt entire-brain binary (skips go build)
#
# Evidence: a timestamped pass/fail summary (with brain/graph/host versions)
# is written under .smoke-evidence/ with host paths redacted.
set -euo pipefail

repo_root=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)
evidence_dir=${SMOKE_EVIDENCE_DIR:-"$repo_root/.smoke-evidence"}
stamp=$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)
evidence="$evidence_dir/release-smoke-$stamp.md"

REPO_ID=${REPO_ID:?export REPO_ID (staging brainstore repo ULID) -- see header}
API_URL=${API_URL:?export API_URL (staging cell base URL) -- see header}

# Hosted sync fails closed under the egress kill switch; this suite exists to
# exercise egress, so both spellings must be unset.
unset ENTIRE_BRAIN_NO_EGRESS ENTIRE_BRAIN_LOCAL_ONLY
# The claude CLI refuses to start inside another Claude Code session and names
# unsetting CLAUDECODE as the bypass. Distill's child is non-interactive
# (--print), so the bypass is safe; a normal terminal never has this set.
unset CLAUDECODE

command -v git >/dev/null || { echo "FATAL: git is required" >&2; exit 1; }
command -v entire >/dev/null || { echo "FATAL: the entire CLI is required" >&2; exit 1; }
command -v python3 >/dev/null || { echo "FATAL: python3 is required" >&2; exit 1; }
if ! command -v claude >/dev/null && ! command -v codex >/dev/null; then
  echo "FATAL: leg 3 (distill) needs a coding agent on PATH (claude or codex)" >&2
  exit 1
fi

# Released CLIs can print an update banner on stdout; the token is the last
# non-empty line (same rule as the plugin's mintHostedToken).
last_line() { awk 'NF {line=$0} END {print line}'; }
if [ -n "${AUTH_CONTEXT:-}" ]; then
  ENTIRE_TOKEN=REDACTED auth token --context "$AUTH_CONTEXT" | last_line)
else
  ENTIRE_TOKEN=REDACTED auth token | last_line)
fi
export ENTIRE_TOKEN

work=$(mktemp -d)
smoke_branch="smoke-$stamp"
# Each repo lives BESIDE its machine's plugin dirs ($work/<m>/data etc.), never
# inside them: the brain reads `git status` for its dirty gates and freshness
# axes, so state dirs nested in the worktree flood it with the brain's own
# writes — the seed then refuses to build and leg 1's release gate fails on a
# mess the suite itself made. (hosted-sync-smoke.sh still nests; it asserts no
# freshness, so it survives it.)
scratch="$work/a/repo"
clone_b="$work/b/repo"

declare -a leg_names=(
  "1 setup: enable + brain setup healthy"
  "2 capture: commit writes a checkpoint"
  "3 distill: real agent writes >=1 fact"
  "4 recall: distilled fact comes back"
  "5 graph: fixture symbol resolves"
  "6 upload: hosted sync up, fact visible remotely"
  "7 pull: second clone pulls + merges the fact"
)
declare -a leg_status=(not-run not-run not-run not-run not-run not-run not-run)
current_leg=0

#!/bin/bash
#MISE description="Release smoke: full user journey on scratch repos (enable, capture, distill, recall, graph, hosted sync up/down)"
#
# A tripwire, not a test suite: one assert per leg, each fails loudly.
# Legs: 1 setup, 2 checkpoint capture, 3 distill, 4 recall, 5 graph query,
#        6 hosted upload (staging), 7 pull+merge on a second clone.
#
# The entire-brain binary under test is built from this checkout (the RC SHA);
# the host `entire` CLI and the entire-graph provider are the installed ones.
# Brain state is isolated per "machine" via ENTIRE_PLUGIN_*_DIR, like
# scripts/hosted-sync-smoke.sh; HOME and the host CLI's login stay real because
# legs 3 and 6 need the real coding agent and the real staging auth.
#
# Environment the runner must export (legs 6-7; never hardcode secrets):
#   REPO_ID       region-local repo ULID of a STAGING brainstore repo
#   API_URL       that repo's home-cell base URL, e.g. https://<home-cell>.api.partial.to/api/v1
#   AUTH_CONTEXT  optional saved `entire auth` login to mint the token from
#                 (e.g. us.auth.partial.to); default: the active context
#   ENTIRE_BRAIN_BIN  optional prebuilt entire-brain binary (skips go build)
#
# Evidence: a timestamped pass/fail summary (with brain/graph/host versions)
# is written under .smoke-evidence/ with host paths redacted.
set -euo pipefail

repo_root=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)
evidence_dir=${SMOKE_EVIDENCE_DIR:-"$repo_root/.smoke-evidence"}
stamp=$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)
evidence="$evidence_dir/release-smoke-$stamp.md"

REPO_ID=${REPO_ID:?export REPO_ID (staging brainstore repo ULID) -- see header}
API_URL=${API_URL:?export API_URL (staging cell base URL) -- see header}

# Hosted sync fails closed under the egress kill switch; this suite exists to
# exercise egress, so both spellings must be unset.
unset ENTIRE_BRAIN_NO_EGRESS ENTIRE_BRAIN_LOCAL_ONLY
# The claude CLI refuses to start inside another Claude Code session and names
# unsetting CLAUDECODE as the bypass. Distill's child is non-interactive
# (--print), so the bypass is safe; a normal terminal never has this set.
unset CLAUDECODE

command -v git >/dev/null || { echo "FATAL: git is required" >&2; exit 1; }
command -v entire >/dev/null || { echo "FATAL: the entire CLI is required" >&2; exit 1; }
command -v python3 >/dev/null || { echo "FATAL: python3 is required" >&2; exit 1; }

fi

entire-brain is an external-command plugin for the Entire CLI.

It builds a local, inspectable repository brain from retained sessions, seed
context, docs, history, code-index records, and durable memories, then exposes
retrieval, verification, and evaluation surfaces for agents.

Usage:
  entire-brain [flags]
  entire-brain [command]

Set up the brain & agents:
  setup              Build the brain and start background updates
  add                Clone a repository, fetch its Entire history, and build its brain
  agent-guide        Preview repository-specific agent instructions
  webhook            Notify another service when this brain changes
  config             Inspect or initialize plugin configuration

Search & explore the brain:
  overview           Summarize the project, its structure, and decisions
  brief              Gather relevant context for a task
  query              Search the brain (BM25 lexical ranking)
  get                Fetch a brain item by ID
  multi-get          Fetch multiple brain items by ID
  dash               Browse the brain in an interactive dashboard

Durable memories & patterns:
  recall             Retrieve durable memories matching a query for the current branch
  remember           Record a durable memory about this repository
  distill            Extract durable memories from sessions (requires an agent)
  memories           Review, promote, and garbage-collect durable memories
  connect            Bind this repository to its hosted brain explicitly
  disconnect         Stop syncing this repository with its hosted brain
  verify             Verify durable memory anchors against local retained sources
  patterns           Inspect and rebuild recurring patterns from sessions

Code index & context:
  inspect            Explore code, dependencies, and change history
  show               Show one code-index record
  viz                Explore the brain as a graph in your browser

content.content:
--- 84fd0b41 fix(cli): stop hosted facts sync retrying 403 forever on a stale repo binding
A binding written by 'entire brain connect' never refreshed, so once the
bound repo was deleted or the caller lost access, every trigger (session-end
hook, daemon tick, push hint) retried the same 403 indefinitely and tripped
brainstore's auth-failure monitor (COR-2279).

factsync now surfaces 403 as ErrNoAccess. On a pull denial the sync
re-resolves placement once: a different repo id in the same cell (deleted
and re-onboarded) rebinds and retries; otherwise the binding records a 24h
no-access pause that all background triggers skip, with one actionable line
naming connect. connect clears the pause by writing a fresh binding; status
reports it.

A push-only 403 keeps the pull-only degradation: a read-only grant
(push 403, pull 200) is a working state and must keep pulling. Rebind
requires the same cell URL so explicit staging/non-default bindings are
never retargeted. 401 keeps its current behavior so auth-plumbing breaks
still reach the monitor.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Entire-Checkpoint: 01M5Z56KVH7EQ5XMHBZ35WHV4V

--- f1a0bdfb fix(cli): only report a no-access pause that was actually recorded
Review finding on trail 2636: pauseHostedSyncNoAccess printed "sync paused
until …" even when the guarded write declined (a concurrent connect or
disconnect changed the binding) or failed. Now the paused line prints only
after a successful write; a declined write is silent and a failed write
reports the failure with the no-access context.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Entire-Checkpoint: 01M5Z5PD4BMF1P624WMFSE59VZ

--- 98a7c172 fix(doctor): stop flagging staged candidates as a stale facts manifest
summarizeFactSource deliberately declares a factStatusCandidate under
pending_reconcile rather than Facts, but inspectFactStore counted the
same record into Readable and compared Readable against Facts alone. A
brain holding one staged candidate (a crashed distill run's leftover)
therefore reported "memory count does not match the manifest: the
manifest is behind the store — run refresh" permanently: the refresh the
warning recommends re-derives the identical split and the error
survives it.

The cross-check now compares Readable against declared plus
pending_reconcile, and the lossy/stale messages name the staged share
so their arithmetic adds up. A candidate the manifest never summarized
still reports stale, and a genuinely extra active record still trips
the check.

Observed on a real brain: 24591 declared + 7 candidates = 24598
readable, flagged as an error through every refresh.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Entire-Checkpoint: 01M5XC0R3KW2P87C3P2WK93TWJ

## [Unreleased]

## [0.4.0] - 2026-10-27

### Removed

- The local MCP surface: `brain mcp` (stdio and `--http`), the `/v1` REST API
  it mounted, and the Python/TypeScript SDKs with their LangChain/LlamaIndex
  integrations. The CLI is the canonical agent surface — the agent guide
  drives every interaction through `entire brain` verbs, and the MCP tools
  were thin wrappers returning the same `--json` payloads — so the surfaces
  carried ~15k lines and an HTTP listener with bearer tokens that SECURITY.md
  had to reason about, with no recorded dependency. `capabilities` no longer
  reports an `mcp` feature. The CLI behavior `docs/semantic_mcp_guide.md`
  described stays, rewritten as `docs/semantic_features.md`.

### Fixed

- Hosted facts sync no longer retries a 403 forever against a stale repo
  binding (COR-2279: deleted or access-revoked repos tripped brainstore's
  auth-failure monitor from every session-end hook, daemon tick, and push
  hint). A pull denial now re-resolves placement once — a repo deleted and
  re-onboarded in the same cell rebinds and retries — and otherwise records
  a 24h no-access pause that background triggers skip, with one actionable
  line naming `connect`. A push-only 403 (read-only grant) keeps pulling,
  and 401 still reaches the monitor.

- The no-access pause unwinds on its own once access returns: a successful
  hosted pull retires the recorded pause, and `status` only reports a pause
  that was actually written and is still in the future. Previously a
  restored grant kept `status` claiming the repo was paused and
  recommending `connect` forever, and a declined pause write still printed
  "sync paused".

- `doctor` and the brief warnings no longer flag a brain holding staged
  distill candidates as a stale facts manifest. The readable-count
  cross-check now includes `pending_reconcile` records, so the
  "memory count does not match the manifest — run refresh" error that
  survived every refresh is gone; the stale/lossy messages name the staged
  share so their arithmetic adds up.

content.text:
**Status:** validation is done and everything is green — the 0.4.0 changelog PR is open and I'm watching its CI; I'll merge and tag `v0.4.0` when it's green.

Validation results (all on release SHA `f56e65ad`, current main HEAD):

- `release:smoke` **7/7 legs passed** against staging — includes the hosted sync up/pull legs that exercise the COR-2279 client-issue fixes.
- Full uncached `go test ./...` clean; `gofmt -l -s` + `go vet` clean (the real CI gate).
- All six release targets + the pure-Go default build compile with `CGO_ENABLED=0`.
- Post-reorg command check: diffed the entire subcommand tree of a freshly built v0.3.0 binary vs HEAD — identical except `mcp`, which was removed intentionally ("Remove the local MCP surface", 9d3f08e3).
- CI on main HEAD: all 23 jobs green, including both benchmark jobs.

One thing that looked scary but isn't: local `mise run release:readiness` fails several evidence lanes, but every failure traces to this machine's Python 3.9 (`fromisoformat` can't parse `Z` timestamps, no `tomllib`) — CI runs the same lanes on Python 3.12/3.14 and is green on this exact SHA, and evidence re-proof was deliberately taken off the tag path in 0.3.0. Saved a memory note so this doesn't bite again.

Release prep: opened **PR #548** (https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/548) with the dated `[0.4.0] - 2026-10-27` changelog section covering the MCP-surface removal (why it's 0.4.0, not 0.3.1), the three COR-2279 hosted-sync no-access fixes, and the doctor staged-candidates fix. Once its CI is green I'll merge, tag the merge commit `v0.4.0`, and push the tag — `release.yml` builds, verifies Windows, and publishes from there. Say the word if you'd rather do the merge/tag yourself.
